_link.title: I can explain the relationship between temperature and rate of reaction using collision theory

toLevel2.stem: What effect does increasing temperature have on the kinetic energy of particles?
distractors: It decreases their kinetic energy
It has no effect on kinetic energy
It only changes their orientation

toLevel2.stem: Increasing temperature affects which aspects of collision theory?
toLevel2.answer: Both collision frequency and collision energy
distractors: Collision frequency only
Collision energy only
Particle orientation only

toLevel2.stem: What happens to the proportion of particles with energy greater than the activation energy when temperature increases?
distractors: It decreases
It stays the same
It drops to zero

toLevel2.stem: Why does increasing temperature increase collision frequency?
toLevel2.answer: Particles move faster and collide more often
distractors: More particles are created at higher temperatures
The container becomes smaller at higher temperatures
The activation energy is reduced by the heat

toLevel2.stem: Increasing temperature leads to a faster reaction rate because:
toLevel2.answer: more collisions occur and more of them exceed the activation energy
distractors: the activation energy of the reaction is lowered by heat
the particles change to a more favourable orientation
the total number of particles in the system increases

toLevel2.stem: Increasing temperature increases both the frequency and the energy of particle collisions.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: Temperature only affects collision frequency and has no effect on the energy of collisions.
distractors: True

toLevel3.stem: Why is temperature considered particularly powerful for changing reaction rate compared to concentration?
toLevel3.answer: It affects both collision frequency and the proportion of particles exceeding Ea
distractors: It only affects collision frequency, the same as concentration does
It lowers the activation energy of the reaction permanently
It changes the orientation of particles during every collision

toLevel3.stem: How does increased kinetic energy at higher temperature lead to more successful collisions?
toLevel3.answer: More particles have enough energy to overcome the activation energy barrier
distractors: Particles align in the correct orientation more easily at higher temperature
The activation energy is eliminated when temperature is high enough
Faster particles are smaller and can fit together more precisely

toLevel3.stem: Why does increasing temperature also increase collision frequency, not just collision energy?
toLevel3.answer: Faster-moving particles cover more distance and encounter each other more often
distractors: Higher temperature creates additional particles in the reaction mixture
The container shrinks at higher temperature pushing particles together
Particles become larger at higher temperature and overlap more often

toLevel3.stem: A student states that temperature increases reaction rate only by making particles collide more often. What has they overlooked?
toLevel3.answer: Temperature also increases the proportion of particles with energy exceeding Ea
distractors: Temperature also changes the orientation of particles during collisions
Temperature also decreases the activation energy of the reaction
Temperature also reduces the number of particles in the system

toLevel3.stem: Which effect of temperature on collision theory is more significant for increasing rate?
toLevel3.answer: The increased proportion of particles exceeding Ea has a greater effect
distractors: The increased collision frequency is always the dominant effect
Both effects always contribute equally to the rate increase
Neither effect is significant compared to orientation changes

toLevel3.stem: How does temperature differ from concentration in its effect on collision theory?
toLevel3.answer: Temperature affects both frequency and energy; concentration affects frequency only
distractors: Temperature affects frequency only; concentration affects both frequency and energy
Both affect only collision frequency through exactly the same mechanism
Temperature affects orientation; concentration affects energy of collisions

toLevel3.stem: The more significant effect of temperature on rate is the increased proportion of particles with energy exceeding the activation energy.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: Temperature affects {{blank:1}} aspects of collision theory, while concentration and surface area affect only collision {{blank:2}}.
distractors: one

distractors: number

toLevel3.stem: Faster-moving particles at higher temperature cover more {{blank:1}} per unit time, which increases collision {{blank:2}}.
distractors: mass

toLevel4.stem: Hydrochloric acid is heated from 20°C to 40°C before adding calcium carbonate. Using collision theory, explain the faster rate.
toLevel4.answer: More HCl particles have kinetic energy exceeding Ea and collisions are more frequent
distractors: Heating the acid lowers the activation energy of the reaction
Heating creates more HCl particles in the solution
Heating improves the orientation of HCl particles during collisions

toLevel4.stem: A student places one beaker of reactants in ice water (5°C) and another at room temperature (25°C). Both have the same concentration. Which beaker will react faster and why?
toLevel4.answer: The 25°C beaker — particles have higher kinetic energy and collide more frequently
distractors: The 5°C beaker — cold particles collide with more force per collision
Both react at the same rate since the concentration is identical
The 5°C beaker — particles move more slowly and align better

toLevel4.stem: A food chemist stores perishable goods at 4°C to slow spoilage reactions. Using collision theory, which factor is most reduced?
toLevel4.answer: The proportion of particles with energy exceeding Ea for spoilage reactions
distractors: The number of food molecules available to react with oxygen
The activation energy of the spoilage reactions in the food
The orientation of particles involved in decomposition reactions

toLevel4.stem: A student increases the temperature of a reaction from 300 K to 310 K and observes the rate approximately doubles. Which collision theory explanation is most complete?
toLevel4.answer: Both increased frequency and a greater proportion exceeding Ea contribute to the rate doubling
distractors: The activation energy has been halved by the temperature increase
Only the increased collision frequency accounts for the doubling
The 10 K increase eliminates the need for correct orientation

toLevel4.stem: A student wants to speed up a reaction but cannot change the concentration. They decide to heat the reaction mixture. Which collision theory factors will be affected?
toLevel4.answer: Both collision frequency and the proportion of particles exceeding Ea
distractors: Only collision frequency, identical to the effect of concentration
Only the orientation of particle collisions in the mixture
Only the activation energy, which will be reduced by heating

toLevel4.stem: An exothermic reaction between two solutions proceeds slowly at 15°C. A student heats the mixture to 45°C and the reaction proceeds rapidly. Using collision theory, what two changes explain this?
toLevel4.answer: Particles collide more often and a larger proportion have energy exceeding Ea
distractors: The reaction becomes endothermic and absorbs the extra heat energy
The activation energy decreases and the orientation requirement is removed
More reactant particles are created and the products decompose faster

toLevel4.stem: A student writes: 'Heating the reactants from 25°C to 50°C increases rate because the activation energy decreases.' Is this explanation correct?
toLevel4.answer: No — temperature increases particle energy but does not change the activation energy
distractors: Yes — heating always lowers the activation energy of any reaction
No — heating decreases rate because particles move too fast to react
Yes — activation energy is inversely proportional to temperature

toLevel4.stem: Refrigerating food slows spoilage because at lower temperatures, fewer particles have energy exceeding the {{blank:1}} energy of decomposition {{blank:2}}.
distractors: kinetic
processes
potential
pathways

distractors: orientation

toLevel4.stem: Temperature does not change the {{blank:1}} energy of a reaction; instead it increases the {{blank:2}} energy of the reacting particles.
distractors: kinetic

toLevel5.stem: A 10°C rise in temperature roughly doubles the rate of many reactions. Which collision theory factor accounts for most of this increase?
toLevel5.answer: The increased proportion of particles with energy exceeding Ea
distractors: The increased collision frequency from faster-moving particles
The improved orientation of particles at higher temperature
The decreased activation energy caused by the temperature rise

toLevel5.stem: Compare the effects of doubling concentration versus increasing temperature by 10°C on reaction rate. Which analysis is correct?
toLevel5.answer: Doubling concentration roughly doubles frequency; a 10°C rise can double rate through both frequency and energy effects
distractors: Both changes affect only collision frequency and have identical effects
Doubling concentration has a greater effect because it doubles all collision factors
Temperature changes have no measurable effect compared to concentration

toLevel5.stem: A student claims: 'Temperature is the best way to increase reaction rate because it affects two collision theory factors.' Evaluate this reasoning.
toLevel5.answer: The reasoning is sound, but practical constraints like decomposition at high temperature may limit its usefulness
distractors: The reasoning is flawed because temperature only affects one collision theory factor
The reasoning is flawed because catalysts affect more collision theory factors than temperature
The reasoning is sound and temperature is always the best option regardless of circumstances

toLevel5.stem: At very high temperatures, a reaction that normally produces one product begins to produce a different product. How does collision theory help explain this?
toLevel5.answer: More particles now exceed the higher Ea of an alternative reaction pathway
distractors: High temperature eliminates the activation energy for all possible reactions
High temperature changes the orientation requirement to favour different products
High temperature destroys the original reactant particles creating new ones

toLevel5.stem: A peer states: 'Since temperature increases collision frequency, it works the same way as increasing concentration.' Is this comparison valid?
toLevel5.answer: No — temperature additionally increases the proportion of particles exceeding Ea
distractors: Yes — both factors affect only collision frequency in identical ways
No — concentration increases collision energy while temperature does not
Yes — both factors affect collision frequency and energy equally

toLevel5.stem: A reaction with a very high activation energy barely proceeds at 25°C but proceeds moderately at 100°C. Using collision theory, why is the temperature effect so dramatic?
toLevel5.answer: At 25°C almost no particles exceed the high Ea; at 100°C a significant proportion do
distractors: At 100°C the activation energy is reduced to near zero by the heat
At 25°C particles cannot collide at all due to insufficient movement
At 100°C all particles have identical kinetic energy exceeding Ea

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that cooling a reaction mixture should be avoided in all industrial processes because it slows the rate. Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — some reactions must be cooled to prevent unwanted side reactions or decomposition
distractors: Correct — cooling always reduces efficiency and should never be used
Incorrect — cooling increases the rate by improving particle orientation
Correct — industrial processes always benefit from the highest possible temperature

toLevel5.stem: Two reactions have different activation energies. When temperature is increased by 10°C, Reaction X (high Ea) shows a greater rate increase than Reaction Y (low Ea). Why?
toLevel5.answer: For high Ea reactions, the tail of the energy distribution is more sensitive to temperature changes
distractors: High Ea reactions have their activation energy reduced more by temperature increases
Low Ea reactions are unaffected by temperature because most particles already exceed Ea
High Ea reactions create more particles when temperature increases

distractors: Ek
